---
name: commit-message
description: Use when the user asks to commit, submit, or save changes. Check the scope of the changes first, propose an English commit message in this project's format, and only commit after the user confirms.
---

# Commit message rules

Format: `<type>: <one sentence describing what was done>`

## Types

- feat: new feature
- fix: bug fix
- style: visual tweaks (no logic changes)
- docs: documentation (SPEC, DESIGN, CLAUDE.md, etc.)
- refactor: refactoring (same behavior)
- test: tests
- chore: chores (config, packages, etc.)

## Rules

- Read git status and the diff first, and list the files you plan to commit; don't automatically add every untracked file
- If you see `.env`, keys, credentials, or a file you can't figure out, stop and flag it
- Propose the commit message and scope first, and only run git add and git commit after the user confirms
- Write the description in English and say "what was done," not "which file changed"
- For fix, the description should include the cause, so it's easier to dig through history later
- One commit per thing; if things got mixed together, split them first

## Examples

- feat: add a spending stats page with a pie chart
- fix: delete by id to avoid index mismatch after sorting

Some of you might be wondering: why not just load the whole Skill from the start, instead of matching the user's request against the
It keeps the context from getting flooded

The AI doesn't normally spread every skill's full text out on the desk (that would eat way too much context). It only sees the names and descriptions, uses those to decide "does the current task need this one?", and only opens up the full content when there's a match.

Notice anything? I'm teaching the AI the way I'd teach a person. This three-part structure is exactly the same as the "SOP for teaching people" we talked about earlier. For AI, examples work especially well. Following a template is way more reliable for it than reasoning from rules, so never skip the examples when you write a skill.

So when should you turn something into a Skill? My rule of thumb: if you've said the same thing three or more times, write it up as a Skill, so you don't have to keep repeating yourself.
